extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students of literature, playwrights and screenwriters studying comic genres
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating or analysing works in the comedy of manners genre — a realistic, satirical form that critiques social conventions through character types and witty dialogue across plays, novels, film, and television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre definition: realistic, satirical examination of manners and social conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In English literature, the term comedy of manners (also anti-sentimental comedy) describes a genre of realistic, satirical comedy that questions and comments upon the manners and social conventions of a greatly sophisticated, artificial society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead frames the genre as social critique set in an urbane/sophisticated milieu; useful as a canonical definition when deciding whether a work belongs to this genre. Examples referenced: The Importance of Being Earnest (Oscar Wilde).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim: satire of fashion, manners, and outlook of social classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The satire of fashion, manners, and outlook on life of the social classes is a central feature of the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should target class-based pretensions and fashions; the social classes' outlook and behaviour are the objects of ridicule or examination. The page notes this is 'realised with stock characters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stock characters (fop, rake, braggart soldier, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The satire is realised with stock characters, such as the braggart soldier of Ancient Greek comedy, and the fop and the rake of English Restoration comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including recognizable character types that embody particular social affectations helps signal the genre. Historical exemplars: Menander, Plautus, Terence, Restoration playwrights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witty, epigrammatic dialogue as the primary vehicle for commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: The social commentary is thematically presented through the witty dialogue of the characters; the genre is associated with epigrammatic, clever speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise sharp, pithy lines and repartee; dialogue should reveal hypocrisy and manners. Example given: Oscar Wilde's plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot is often clever/scandalous but secondary to social commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: The clever plot of a comedy of manners (often a scandal) is secondary to the social commentary thematically presented through the witty dialogue of the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing a piece, ensure that any intricate or scandal-driven plot serves to expose manners/hypocrisy rather than being the primary focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradition of elaborate, artificial plotting paired with epigrammatic dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The tradition of elaborate, artificial plotting, and epigrammatic dialogue was carried on by later playwrights like Oscar Wilde.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emulate an 'artificial' or stylised plotting approach that creates situations for social satire, while maintaining verbally sharp dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target themes: hypocrisies and pretensions (sexual, moral, class-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays and works in the genre commonly satirise the hypocrisies and pretensions of ruling orders or social morality (e.g., Molière satirising the ancien régime; Wilde satirising sexual hypocrisies of Victorian morality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topical or period-specific hypocrisies and pretensions as the thematic focus; sexual morality and class pretension are frequent targets in canonical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and register: verbal dexterity and wit, with potential for crude eruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre displays the verbal dexterity one associates with witty playwrights; however, 'the patina of wit occasionally erupts into shocking crudity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for high verbal skill and polished wit, but be aware a work may intentionally verge into cruder humor for effect — use deliberately and in service of satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium flexibility: applicable across plays, novels, film, and television
rubrics_metrics.description: Many works categorized as 'comedy of manners' are novels or plays, but the genre also exists in film and television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defining traits (satire of manners, stock characters, witty dialogue) can be adapted to different media; examples: The Dinner Game (film), Curb Your Enthusiasm (television), Jeeves and Wooster (stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/lineage markers: New Comedy, Roman imitation, Restoration, Molière, Congreve, Wilde, Coward
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre originated in the New Comedy period (325–260 BC) of Classical Greece (Menander), was imitated by Roman playwrights (Plautus, Terence), flourished in the Restoration period (Wycherley, Congreve), and was carried on by Molière, Oscar Wilde, Noël Coward, and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with historical forms and predecessors informs faithful use of conventions and recognisable callbacks; creators/analysts may situate works along this lineage when classifying or crafting comedies of manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variant labels and related subgenres (anti-sentimental comedy, comedy of menace)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'comedy of manners' is also called 'anti-sentimental comedy' historically; related/wordplay variants like 'comedy of menace' exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of alternate labels and playful subgenre names; these signal shifts in tone or intention (e.g., anti-sentimental critiques vs. menacing/darker comic effects) and can guide classification.
